newsitem.title: IRAQ: Oil money to flow into Iraq's escrow account soon.
newsitem.headline: Oil money to flow into Iraq's escrow account soon.

text.p: Money from partial oil exports under Iraq's oil-for-food formula with the United Nations is to flow into Baghdad's escrow acount by mid January, a senior oil official said on Tuesday.

Saddam al-Hassan chairman of the State Organisation for the Marketing of Oil (SOMO) said Iraq had given foreign firms purchasing its oil under the deal about a month to tranfer the money to the account in the New York branch of the French Banque Nationale de Paris.
"Buyers have one month to send the money. First amounts should be there by the fifteenth or sixteenth of this month," Hassan told Reuters.

He would not discolose how much money would be sent to the account by the middle of the month but said SOMO's contracts with foreign companies were enough for the money Iraq was allowed to obtain in six months.
Iraq started partial exports in December 10. It has found no difficulty in meeting its U.N. renewable quota of $2 billion in six months.
Hassan said Iraq stopped signing deals with foreign firms for about ten days ago though it had the ability to export much more oil than it is allowed.
"Once the money pours into the escrow account Iraq can start buying foodstuffs and medical supplies," he said.
The U.N. sanctions committee has not so far approved any Iraqi contract to buy humanitarian supplies despite the rush by foreign businessmen to strike such deals.

Diplomats in Baghdad said the first sums would be earmarked for the stationing of 151 international staff in Baghdad whom the U.S. would like to see in position before any food or medicine from the oil deal starts arriving in the country.

Officials from the trade ministry have travelled to southeastern Asian countries to prepare for the shipment of rice, sugar, cooking oil and other commodities to Iraq once the money from the oil deal is made available.
Trade officials said several countries were ready to supply Iraq with humanitarian goods and be paid later from the oil money but the sanctions committee balked at such arrangement.
Some 14 oil monitors from the Netherlands-based Saybolt inspection firm are in place in both Iraq and Turkey but none of the food observers has arrived yet.
Iraq has earmarked more than $800 million for food purchases and and $210 million for medical supplies.
